title: Dermatology and Venereology
description: Skin structure and lesions, infections and infestations, eczema and psoriasis, pigmentary disorders and skin bleaching, HIV-related skin disease, and sexually transmitted infections.

topics.title: Describing Skin Disease
topics.summary: Primary and secondary lesions, distribution, and skin examination in dark skin.

notes.b: Primary lesions: macule (flat, < 1 cm colour change) and patch (> 1 cm), papule (raised, < 1 cm) and plaque (> 1 cm, flat-topped), nodule (deeper, > 1 cm), vesicle (fluid, < 1 cm) and bulla (> 1 cm), pustule (pus), wheal (transient oedematous — urticaria). Secondary changes: scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, excoriation, lichenification (thickened skin from chronic scratching), atrophy, scar and keloid. Also describe colour, shape (annular, target), arrangement (linear — Koebner phenomenon, grouped — herpes), distribution (flexural, extensor, photo-exposed, dermatomal), and involvement of hair, nails and mucosae. In dark skin, erythema appears violaceous or darker brown rather than red, and post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation is common and distressing. Investigations: skin scrapings with KOH for fungi, Wood's lamp, swabs, and skin biopsy.
k: Erythema looks violaceous in dark skin

notes.b: Surveys in Nigerian dermatology clinics show infections (fungal — tinea, pityriasis versicolor; bacterial — impetigo, folliculitis; viral — warts, molluscum; scabies) dominate in children and rural areas, while eczema (atopic, contact), acne vulgaris, pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, complications of skin bleaching), urticaria, pseudofolliculitis barbae and keloids are common in adults. Traction alopecia (tight braiding) and central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia are common hair problems in women. Many patients self-medicate with potent topical steroid–antifungal–antibiotic combination creams sold over the counter, which cause tinea incognito, acne, striae and atrophy.
k: Eczema, acne, pigmentary disorders in adults

topics.title: Skin Infections and Infestations
topics.summary: Bacterial, fungal and viral skin infections, scabies, and cutaneous manifestations of leprosy.

notes.b: Impetigo (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes — honey-coloured crusts; bullous impetigo from staphylococci): topical fusidic acid or mupirocin; oral flucloxacillin for extensive disease; post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow. Folliculitis, furuncles (boils) and carbuncles (drain; check for diabetes if recurrent). Cellulitis and erysipelas (penicillin or flucloxacillin). Dermatophytoses: tinea capitis (children — scaling, broken hair, kerion; needs oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, not topical therapy alone), tinea corporis (annular scaly plaques with active edge), tinea cruris, pedis and unguium (onychomycosis). Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia; hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly macules on the trunk; selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo, topical azoles). Candidiasis (intertrigo, oral thrush — consider HIV and diabetes).

Viral: warts (HPV), molluscum contagiosum (umbilicated papules — extensive in HIV), herpes simplex (grouped vesicles), herpes zoster (dermatomal painful vesicles — in young adults suggests HIV; acyclovir within 72 hours; post-herpetic neuralgia), chickenpox and mpox. Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei mite; intensely itchy at night; burrows in finger webs, wrists, genitals, and nipples; household members affected): treat all contacts simultaneously with permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate (or oral ivermectin), wash bedding; crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunosuppressed patients is highly contagious. Head lice (pediculosis). Cutaneous larva migrans (serpiginous track from dog/cat hookworm larvae — walking barefoot on sand; albendazole). Leprosy: hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, thickened nerves; MDT. Buruli ulcer and cutaneous leishmaniasis are other tropical skin infections.
k: Zoster in young adult: test HIV

topics.title: Eczema, Psoriasis, Acne and Urticaria
topics.summary: Inflammatory skin diseases and their management.

notes.b: Atopic eczema (dermatitis): itchy, dry skin with flexural involvement in older children (face and extensors in infants), associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis; in black skin, follicular (papular) eczema and pigment change are common. Management: emollients (liberally), avoid irritants (harsh soaps), topical corticosteroids (appropriate potency — mild for the face, stronger for thick plaques, for limited periods), treat secondary infection. Contact dermatitis: irritant (detergents, hair products) or allergic (nickel, rubber, hair dyes — paraphenylenediamine, cosmetics; patch testing). Seborrhoeic dermatitis is common and may be severe in HIV. Psoriasis: well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp and nails (pitting, onycholysis); Koebner phenomenon; associated with arthritis and metabolic syndrome; can flare in HIV. Treatment: emollients, topical steroids, vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), coal tar, phototherapy, methotrexate and biologics for severe disease.
k: Psoriasis: silvery scale, extensors, nail pitting

notes.b: Acne vulgaris (comedones, papules, pustules, nodules; post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and keloidal scars in dark skin): topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide, topical or oral antibiotics (doxycycline) with benzoyl peroxide to prevent resistance, combined pills in women, and isotretinoin for severe acne (teratogenic — strict contraception). Acne may be induced by steroids and cosmetics (pomade acne). Urticaria (itchy transient wheals < 24 h): acute (foods, drugs, infections) or chronic (> 6 weeks); non-sedating antihistamines; angioedema with airway involvement or anaphylaxis — adrenaline. Serious cutaneous drug reactions: Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (mucosal erosions, skin detachment with positive Nikolsky sign — sulfonamides (cotrimoxazole), nevirapine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, allopurinol; stop drug, supportive burns-type care), DRESS (fever, rash, eosinophilia, organ involvement) and fixed drug eruptions (recurring at the same site — common with sulfonamides and NSAIDs). Drug reactions are more frequent in people with HIV.

topics.title: Pigmentary Disorders, Skin Bleaching and Keloids
topics.summary: Vitiligo, melasma, albinism, skin-lightening complications and keloids.

notes.b: Vitiligo: autoimmune loss of melanocytes causing depigmented (milk-white) patches, often symmetrical (hands, face, genitals), highly visible and stigmatising in dark skin; associated with thyroid disease; treated with topical steroids or calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy, camouflage and psychological support. Melasma: symmetrical brown patches on the face in women (pregnancy, hormonal contraception, sun exposure) — sun protection, hydroquinone (short courses under supervision), azelaic acid. Oculocutaneous albinism (autosomal recessive absence of melanin; prevalence higher in Nigeria than in many regions): pale skin and hair, nystagmus, photophobia and poor vision; very high risk of sun damage and squamous cell carcinoma at young ages — strict sun protection (clothing, hats, sunscreen), regular skin checks, low-vision support and protection from discrimination. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation follows acne, eczema and injury.

Skin bleaching (use of skin-lightening products) is widespread in Nigeria (WHO reported high prevalence among Nigerian women). Products contain hydroquinone (exogenous ochronosis — paradoxical blue-black pigmentation), potent topical corticosteroids (skin atrophy, striae, acne, infections, delayed wound healing, and systemic effects — Cushing's syndrome, adrenal suppression, diabetes, hypertension), and mercury (nephrotoxicity — nephrotic syndrome, neurological damage). Complications also include difficulty with surgical wound healing and skin cancer. Nigeria's NAFDAC restricts hydroquinone above 2% and mercury-containing products; public education is essential. Keloids (scar tissue extending beyond the original wound; common in people of African descent — ear piercing, acne, surgery, tribal marks; chest, shoulders, earlobes): intralesional triamcinolone injections, silicone sheets, pressure therapy, cryotherapy, surgical excision combined with steroids or radiotherapy (recurrence is common after excision alone). Hypertrophic scars stay within the wound margins and often regress.

topics.title: HIV-related Skin Disease and Sexually Transmitted Infections
topics.summary: Skin signs of HIV, Kaposi sarcoma, genital ulcers and discharges, and syphilis.

notes.b: Skin disease is often the first sign of HIV. Suggestive conditions: herpes zoster (especially multidermatomal or in young adults), pruritic papular eruption (intensely itchy papules on limbs — common in Africa), seborrhoeic dermatitis (severe), oral candidiasis and oral hairy leukoplakia, extensive molluscum and warts, recurrent or chronic herpes simplex ulcers, eosinophilic folliculitis, and drug eruptions (cotrimoxazole, nevirapine — SJS/TEN). Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8): violaceous macules, plaques and nodules on skin, mouth (palate), lymph nodes and viscera; lymphoedema; diagnosis by biopsy; treatment is ART plus chemotherapy (paclitaxel, bleomycin–vincristine) for advanced disease. IRIS can worsen skin conditions after starting ART. Cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis may cause molluscum-like umbilicated papules in advanced HIV.

Genital ulcer disease: syphilis (Treponema pallidum — painless indurated chancre; secondary — rash on palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches; tertiary — gummas, cardiovascular and neurosyphilis; congenital syphilis — stillbirth, snuffles, rash, Hutchinson's teeth; treat with benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM; test all pregnant women), chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi — painful, ragged ulcer with suppurative inguinal buboes; azithromycin or ceftriaxone), genital herpes (painful recurrent vesicles and ulcers — acyclovir), lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia L1–L3 — inguinal buboes, 'groove sign'; doxycycline) and donovanosis. Urethral discharge in men: gonorrhoea (purulent; Gram-negative intracellular diplococci; ceftriaxone plus azithromycin due to rising resistance) and chlamydia (doxycycline). Genital warts (HPV 6/11). Principles: syndromic management, partner notification and treatment, HIV and syphilis testing, condom promotion and follow-up. Ulcers increase HIV transmission.
